Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette:
Elena had spent twenty-seven years as a detective, most of them in the homicide division, but nothing had prepared her for the morning she walked into that abandoned basement on the South Side. The call had been routine-a suspicious death, possible overdose-but the moment she descended the stairs, the air changed. A chemical smell, sharp and sweet, hit her sinuses before she could register what it was. Within minutes, her throat closed, her lungs seized, and she was on her hands and knees, gasping, while younger officers pulled her backward up the steps. After the image broke through again-the cold concrete, the chemical sweetness-she caught herself thinking: if this could happen on a routine call, then there was no such thing as safety, and the department she had given her life to had been lying to her all along. The hospital later said it was a concentrated mix of industrial solvents, illegally stored. She spent three days in the ICU, two more on oxygen. The doctors told her she would be fine. Elena did not believe them.

In the months that followed, the memory of that basement refused to behave like a normal memory. It arrived in fragments-the cold concrete against her palms, the ringing in her ears, the face of the officer who grabbed her arm-but never in sequence, never as a whole story she could hold in her mind. She would start to recall the sound of her own breathing, the way it had turned into a wet rattle, and then something would slam shut inside her, pushing the rest away before she could reach it. When the memory did break through, it felt less like remembering and more like being pulled back into that moment, her chest tightening, her skin prickling, the present dissolving around her.

She found herself avoiding the precinct gym because the smell of sweat from the locker room made her stomach turn, and she started taking the stairs instead of the elevator because the antiseptic scent near the second-floor clinic sent her heart racing. When she heard an unexpected sound-a door slamming, a car backfiring-her whole body would lock, her muscles bracing for a threat she could not name. She began scanning every room she entered, checking exits, watching faces, her body perpetually coiled. She had come to believe that she could never let her guard down again, that the institutions she had trusted-the department, the hospital, the safety protocols she had once believed in-had failed her completely. This conviction that she had been betrayed by the very systems meant to protect her kept dragging her back to the moment of collapse, as if the memory itself was the proof she needed to hold onto. What was the point of procedure if it could not keep a veteran detective from nearly dying in a routine call?

Elena started covering her face with her hands whenever she felt short of breath, pressing her palms against her cheeks and nose as if she could block out the world. She learned to redirect her thoughts when the memories threatened to surface, forcing herself to think of case files, grocery lists, anything else. Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day-pressing her palms to her face, scanning every room for exits-she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it, which only confirmed what she already feared: that she was no longer the detective she had been. But not talking about it, never letting the story fully form in her mind, meant the memory had never been put anywhere-it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, and when it did surface it came with all the force of something that had been waiting. She avoided her captain, ducking into stairwells when she saw his uniform approaching, because the sight of authority now felt like a promise of betrayal. She was certain that if she stopped being vigilant, if she let herself relax even for a moment, something terrible would happen again-and this time, no one would save her. The more she avoided, the more the memories seemed to press in, demanding attention in fragmented bursts that left her dizzy and ashamed. She began to wonder if she had lost something essential, some capacity for normal feeling that other people still possessed.

Her job became a minefield. Every interview in a closed room triggered a flicker of panic. Every hospital visit to a witness sent her pulse into her throat. She started delegating more cases, then avoiding the squad room altogether, working from home on administrative tasks. Her colleagues noticed. Her captain called her in for a wellness check, and Elena sat in his office with her hands clenched under her thighs, unable to look at his badge. She told him she was fine. She was not fine.

What finally brought her to a therapist was a Tuesday morning in the precinct parking lot, when a civilian's car backfired and she dropped to the ground, covering her head, gasping for air she could not catch. A younger officer helped her up. Everyone was watching. That night, alone in her apartment, Elena realized she could not keep living this way-always scanning, always bracing, always one unexpected smell or sound away from being dragged back into that basement. She was afraid of what would happen if she stopped being afraid. But she was more afraid of what would happen if she did not.

violations.explanation: Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., belief that institutions failed her) cause or influence her intrusive memory.
Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory leads to her negative appraisals (e.g., distrust in institutions).
Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that her avoidance or other maladaptive strategies cause or increase the memory intrusions.
Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that her maladaptive strategies (e.g., covering face, redirecting thoughts) cause or reinforce her negative appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., belief that institutions failed her) cause or influence her intrusive memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory leads to her negative appraisals (e.g., distrust in institutions).
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that her avoidance or other maladaptive strategies cause or increase the memory intrusions.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that her maladaptive strategies (e.g., covering face, redirecting thoughts) cause or reinforce her negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
